notes.meaning: Nadab and Abihu, the two oldest sons of Aaron, took firepans and burned incense before the Lord. Instead of taking sacred coals from the bronze altar as God commanded, they used unauthorized, ordinary fire. They acted rashly and entered God's presence on their own terms rather than His.

differ.view: This event shows that God only permits worship that He has expressly commanded in Scripture, and believers must not introduce their own ideas or practices into worship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older Catholic writers saw this sin as a severe earthly lesson in exact obedience, while piously holding that their fault may have been venial and pardoned before death.

notes.meaning: Fire flashed out from the Lord's presence and struck both men dead on the spot. The blaze took their lives like lightning, yet left their bodies and garments unharmed. The very fire that had recently signaled God's pleasure on the altar now revealed His swift judgment against irreverence.

Moses explained that God had declared He will be treated as holy by those who draw near to serve Him. When leaders fail to honor God by obedience, He will display His glory through His righteous judgments. Aaron heard this and remained completely silent, humbly accepting God's justice despite his broken heart.

Moses summoned Mishael and Elzaphan, cousins of Aaron from the family of Kohath. Aaron and his remaining sons were serving at the altar and could not touch dead bodies without becoming ceremonially unclean. Moses ordered the cousins to carry their deceased relatives away from the front of the sanctuary.

The two cousins obeyed Moses and carried the dead men outside the camp by their priestly tunics. The clothing was buried with them because it had become defiled by contact with death and divine judgment. Moving the bodies outside the camp kept the living community clean from ceremonial contamination.

Moses ordered Aaron and his surviving sons not to unbind their hair or tear their clothes in public mourning. If God's anointed priests showed signs of protest, the people might think they questioned God's justice, which would bring wrath upon everyone. The rest of the nation, however, was permitted to openly weep over the loss.

The priests were forbidden to leave the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to attend the burial. The holy anointing oil had dedicated them to the Lord of life, so they could not let family grief interrupt their sacred service. Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar submitted to these hard instructions and stayed at their posts.

The Lord spoke directly to Aaron and commanded that no priest drink wine or beer when entering the Tent of Meeting. Serving under the influence of alcohol was punishable by death and stood as a permanent rule for all future generations. Placing this command right after the tragedy strongly suggests that intoxication may have led to the reckless actions of Nadab and Abihu.

differ.view: The placement of this command immediately after the deaths suggests that Nadab and Abihu had been drinking when they offered unauthorized fire.
Some scholars note there is no certain proof the two sons were drunk, viewing this statute simply as a general rule for sanctuary order.

notes.meaning: Sobriety was required so the priests could clearly distinguish between what is holy and what is ordinary. They also needed sharp judgment to tell what was ceremonially clean from what was unclean. A confused mind could easily lead to careless mistakes in God's presence.

Clear thinking was also necessary so the priests could teach the Israelites all the laws God gave through Moses. The priests were not just altar attendants; they were the nation's spiritual teachers. Leaders must understand God's words thoroughly in order to guide others faithfully.

Moses instructed Aaron and his surviving sons to take the leftover grain offering and eat it without yeast next to the altar. Yeast represented corruption, and this food was considered most holy. Moses gave this reminder so that family grief would not cause the priests to neglect their required sacred meals.

The grain offering had to be eaten within the courtyard of the sanctuary because it was most holy. It belonged by law to Aaron and his sons as their regular portion of the food offerings brought to God. God faithfully provided food for His servants while requiring that holy items remain in holy areas.

Parts of the peace offerings, namely the breast and the thigh, were also assigned to Aaron and his household. Unlike the most holy offerings, these cuts could be eaten in any clean place, and both sons and daughters were allowed to share them. These meals supplied daily food for the priests' entire families.

The people brought the thigh and the breast to the tabernacle along with the fat that was burned on the altar. The priest lifted and waved these pieces before the Lord to show that they belonged to Him before being given to the priestly family. God established this as a lasting rule to sustain the priests throughout their generations.

Moses searched for the goat of the people's sin offering and found that it had been burned up completely instead of eaten. He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar for failing to follow the law. Moses worried that another priestly mistake might bring God's judgment upon the surviving family.

Moses asked why they had failed to eat the most holy sin offering in the sanctuary area. Eating the meat was part of making atonement, which means removing guilt and repairing the people's relationship with God. By eating the sacrifice, the priests visibly showed that God had pardoned the congregation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that eating the purification offering stripped away pagan magical ideas, demonstrating that sin was forgiven by God's promise rather than by ritual magic.

notes.meaning: Moses pointed out that the goat's blood had not been carried inside the Holy Place. By law, only sacrifices whose blood entered the inner room were to be burned outside the camp. Because this blood stayed at the courtyard altar, the priests were supposed to eat the meat as commanded.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars suggest that eating the purification offering removed magical ideas common in ancient religions, showing that cleansing came only from God's word rather than the ritual meat itself.

notes.meaning: Aaron spoke up to answer Moses and explained the heavy sorrow that had struck his home that day. His two eldest sons had just been struck down, and he felt that eating a joyful sacred meal in deep mourning would displease the Lord. Aaron did not act out of rebellion, but out of reverent fear that his sorrow made him unfit.

Moses listened carefully to Aaron's honest explanation and was completely satisfied. He recognized that Aaron was aiming to honor God rather than disobey His commands. The Lord demonstrated mercy to priests who sincerely wanted to please Him, even in the middle of crushing grief.
